analysis.one_liner: Bars federal agencies from requiring lenders to guess a borrower's race from appearance or surname.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in March 2023, referred to the House Financial Services Committee, and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would prohibit any federal agency from requiring a lender, when extending credit, to estimate a borrower's race or ethnicity by visually observing the person or by their surname. Today, when a borrower declines to state their race or ethnicity on a loan application, federal rules let lenders record an estimate based on visual observation or surname; the bill would take that fallback off the table. Supporters framed it as stopping racial profiling at the loan counter; critics of this kind of bill note that those estimates feed the demographic data used to detect lending discrimination. The bill never advanced past its committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Lenders and loan officers benefit most: they would no longer have to make a visual or surname-based guess about an applicant's race when the applicant declines to self-identify, removing an awkward and disputed compliance task. Borrowers who prefer not to have their race noted at all would also be spared that estimate.

how_it_helps.text: The bill states flatly that no federal agency may require anyone extending credit to estimate a borrower's race or ethnicity via visual observation or surname.

Under current federal practice, lenders that collect demographic data for fair-lending reporting may use visual observation or surname when an applicant declines to provide race or ethnicity; the bill would eliminate that method, which its sponsor characterized as profiling.

analysis.who_pays: The cost falls on fair-lending oversight. When borrowers decline to self-identify, forbidding visual or surname estimates leaves gaps in the demographic data that regulators and civil-rights enforcers use to spot patterns of discrimination in mortgage and credit markets. Those gaps would most affect the communities the data is meant to protect.

drawbacks.text: Demographic data collected under federal fair-lending rules is what lets regulators and researchers detect discrimination in lending; removing the visual-observation and surname fallback when applicants decline to self-identify would make that data less complete and discrimination harder to demonstrate.
The bill is a single provision with no replacement mechanism, so agencies would have no alternative way to fill in missing demographic data when borrowers choose not to answer.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real point on the supporters' side: asking a loan officer to judge an applicant's race by looking at them is uncomfortable and can feel like profiling, and borrowers who decline to self-identify arguably should have that choice respected. The cost is that the fallback estimates are part of how fair-lending data gets built, and the bill offers no substitute, so discrimination that shows up in demographic patterns would be harder to catch. On balance, a narrow convenience for lenders comes at the expense of the enforcement record that protects borrowers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and died there — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 27, 2023 by Rep. Roger Williams of Texas, joined by Reps. Blaine Luetkemeyer and French Hill.
On the same day it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
The action history shows no further activity: no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed, so the existing fair-lending data rules stayed in place, which is the outcome enforcement advocates preferred. The bill's sponsor and cosponsors lost nothing either, since the requirement they objected to was never the subject of a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo held; enforcement rules stayed intact

for.name: Rep. Roger Williams
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to bar agencies from requiring visual or surname-based race estimates in lending.

for.name: 2 of 224 House Republicans
for.role: Cosponsors (Reps. Blaine Luetkemeyer and French Hill)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chair Patrick McHenry (R-NC) never scheduled a hearing or markup
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without any hearing, markup, or vote for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Only Republicans backed the bill — the sponsor plus two cosponsors, all Republicans — and since it never came to a vote, no partisan split was ever recorded.

industries.industry: Lenders (banks, mortgage originators, consumer credit providers)
industries.note: If enacted, the bill would spare lenders the task of estimating an applicant's race by appearance or surname when the applicant declines to answer. Its interest runs against the public in this case because those estimates feed the demographic data regulators use to detect lending discrimination, so the lender's relief is the enforcer's blind spot.
